title: Linearising a nonlinear system
objectives: Linearise a nonlinear system at an equilibrium with the Jacobian, as in predator and prey.

screens.title: Predator and prey
screens.prose: Prey $x$ breed and are eaten; predators $y$ starve without prey: $x' = x - 0.5xy$, $y' = -0.75y + 0.25xy$. Drag the start and watch the orbit. An **equilibrium** needs both right sides 0 at once.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which points are equilibria?

options.why: You swapped the coordinates. $x' = 0$ needs $y = 2$, and $y' = 0$ needs $x = 3$.
At $(3, 0)$, $x' = 3 \ne 0$: prey grow with no predators.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set each right side to 0 and solve both together.

explain.text: Either $x = 0$ (then $y = 0$), or $y = 2$ (then $x = 3$). Orbits circle $(3, 2)$, the coexistence point.

screens.title: The Jacobian
screens.prose:
Near an equilibrium, replace each right side by its tangent plane (`multivar` l7). The matrix of partial derivatives is the **Jacobian**, one row per equation:

$$\mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix}1 - 0.5y & -0.5x\\0.25y & -0.75 + 0.25x\end{pmatrix}.$$
screens.question: Write $\mathbf{J}$ at $(3, 2)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $x = 3$, $y = 2$ into each entry.

byKey.origin: That is $\mathbf{J}(0, 0)$. Evaluate at the equilibrium you want, $(3, 2)$.

screens.title: At the origin
screens.prose: At $(0, 0)$ the Jacobian is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-0.75\end{pmatrix}$: prey alone grow, predators alone die. Drag the start close to the origin.
screens.question: What does the linearisation say about $(0, 0)$?

options.why: Only along the $y$ axis. Any prey at all grow away.
The eigenvalues are real, of opposite sign.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the eigenvalues off the diagonal.

explain.text: Real eigenvalues of opposite sign: a saddle, and a saddle is trusted by the nonlinear system too. Extinction of both is not where orbits go.

screens.title: At the coexistence point
screens.question: Enter the eigenvalue with positive imaginary part, exactly.

byKey.real: $\lambda^2 = -0.75$ has no real root; multiply by $i$.

explain.text: $\pm 0.8660i$: the linear system is a centre, with period $2\pi/0.8660 = 7.2552$. The next screen tests that.

screens.title: How far the linear picture holds
screens.prose: The dashed curve follows the linearised system $x' = -1.5(y - 2)$, $y' = 0.5(x - 3)$ from the same start, for one linear period. Drag the start close to $(3, 2)$, then far from it.
screens.question: What is the period of the linear orbits, to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Period is $2\pi$ over the imaginary part.

byKey.true: 7.42 is the true orbit through $(5, 2)$, from a fine-step solve. The linear period is 7.2552.

explain.text: Small orbits take about 7.2552, as the linearisation says. The true orbit through $(5, 2)$ takes about 7.42 and is not an ellipse. The linear picture holds only near the equilibrium.

screens.title: Why the true orbits close
screens.prose: Let $H = 0.25x - 0.75\ln x + 0.5y - \ln y$. Show $H$ is constant along every orbit. One line is wrong; leave it out.
screens.question: Put the argument in order.

lines.text: $= 0$, so each orbit lies on one level curve of $H$, which is closed

lines.why: $x$ and $y$ move with $t$: the chain rule multiplies by $x'$ and $y'$.

hints.text: Use the chain rule on each term of $H$.

feedback.correct: The bracket is 0, so $H$ is conserved.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate along the orbit first, then substitute.

byKey.x: You treated $x$ and $y$ as fixed variables. Along an orbit they change, so multiply by $x'$ and $y'$.

screens.title: Do not trust a linear centre
screens.prose: Add crowding to the prey: $x' = x(1 - cx) - 0.5xy$. At $c = \tfrac16$ the equilibrium moves to $(3, 1)$, with $\mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix}-0.5&-1.5\\0.25&0\end{pmatrix}$. Slide $c$ and watch the path from $(5, 2)$.

screens.question: What happens at $c = \tfrac16$?

options.text: A stable spiral: eigenvalues $-0.25 \pm 0.5590i$, and paths settle at $(3, 1)$
Still a centre, as the uncrowded linearisation said
options.why: You carried the centre over. A centre can change under the smallest nudge; here $\tau = -0.5$.

hints.text: Slide $c$ to its top and read the caption.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\tau$ and $\Delta$ of the new Jacobian.

byKey.c: You trusted the centre. A linear centre decides nothing: a sliver of crowding turns the orbits into an inward spiral.

explain.text: A saddle, node or spiral in the linearisation is trusted near the point (the Hartman-Grobman theorem). A centre is not: the nonlinear terms decide, and here crowding makes paths settle at $(3, 1)$.

screens.title: When the linear test is silent
screens.prose: Take $x' = x^2$, $y' = -y$. At the origin $\mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$: one eigenvalue is 0. Drag starts on the left and on the right.
screens.question: What does the linearisation tell us about the origin?

options.text: Nothing decisive: the zero eigenvalue leaves it to the $x^2$ term
Stable, since the other eigenvalue is $-1$
options.why: From the right, $x' = x^2 > 0$ pushes paths away.

options.text: A line of equilibria, as in lesson 11
options.why: Only the origin is still: at $(1, 0)$, $x' = 1$.
A saddle needs eigenvalues of opposite sign; here one is 0.

hints.text: Its derivative is 0, so the linear system ignores it.

feedback.correct: With a zero eigenvalue the nonlinear term decides: paths arrive from the left and leave to the right.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the linear and the true $x'$ near 0.

explain.text: The linear part says $x' = 0$, but the true $x' = x^2$ is positive on both sides. So the origin attracts from the left and repels on the right.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

# classify(A) from lesson 12 is already defined for you.

def jacobian(f, z, h=1e-6):
    """Central-difference Jacobian of f (which returns a list) at the point z."""
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=float)
    n = len(z)
    J = np.zeros((n, n))
    for k in range(n):
        e = np.zeros(n)
        e[k] = h
        J[:, k] = (np.asarray(f(z + e)) - np.asarray(f(z - e))) / (2 * h)
    return J

def classify_equilibrium(f, z):
    """The type of the equilibrium z of x' = f(x), from its Jacobian."""
    return classify(jacobian(f, z))

screens.title: A cartoon of crowded trades
screens.prose: Read $x$ as alpha left in a trade and $y$ as capital chasing it. Alpha draws capital in; capital eats the alpha; then capital leaves. With the same numbers, this is predator and prey. It is a cartoon, not a fitted model.
screens.question: A small shock knocks the system off $(3, 2)$. What happens?

options.text: It cycles round $(3, 2)$, taking about 7.26 time units a cycle

options.why: Without crowding the orbits close; nothing damps them.
Every orbit with $x, y > 0$ closes, so capital dips but never reaches zero.
$H$ is conserved, so the swings keep their size.

feedback.correct: A centre in the linearisation and a conserved $H$: steady cycles of about 7.26 time units.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what lies round $(3, 2)$.

explain.text: Near $(3, 2)$ the cycle takes about $2\pi/0.866 = 7.26$ time units. Desks linearise nonlinear models for the same reason they compute Greeks: the local linear picture is quick to read.

ideas: At an equilibrium, replace the system by its Jacobian: one row of partial derivatives per equation.
A saddle, node or spiral in the linearisation is trusted near the point. A centre or a zero eigenvalue decides nothing.
Predator and prey conserve $H = 0.25x - 0.75\ln x + 0.5y - \ln y$, so its orbits close; crowding breaks that.

formula.name: Jacobian
formula.tex: \mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix}\partial f_1/\partial x & \partial f_1/\partial y\\ \partial f_2/\partial x & \partial f_2/\partial y\end{pmatrix}
formula.note: Evaluate it at the equilibrium in question.

summary.trap: Trusting a linear centre: the smallest nonlinear term can make it spiral.
